Global Networking

Unit 11 • SL

5 Weeks (15 Lessons) • A

Unit Overview

of Computer Science Unit Foundation Concepts The unit focuses on Interconnectivity and Standardisation. It explores how heterogeneous systems communicate through common rules (Protocols) and the physical and logical architectures required to move data globally. Key themes include the Abstraction of Layers, the Efficiency of Packet Switching, and the Robustness of Digital Defense.

What You'll Learn

  • A2.1: Network types (LAN, WAN, PAN, VPN) and digital infrastructure (Cloud, Edge, Distributed). Functions of devices (Router, Switch, WAP, Gateway) and core protocols (TCP, UDP, HTTP/S, DHCP).
  • A2.2: Topologies (Star, Mesh, Hybrid). Networking models (Client-Server vs. P2P) and logical segmentation (VLANs).
  • A2.3: Transmission media (Fibre, Copper, Wireless). IP Addressing (v4/v6, Static/Dynamic, Public/Private). NAT mechanics and the step-by-step process of Packet Switching.
  • A2.4: Security: Firewalls (filtering rules), Encryption (Symmetric vs. Asymmetric), and the role of Digital Certificates.

Key Terminology

Master these terms to succeed in this unit:

LAN WAN VPN Edge Computing Protocol TCP/IP WAP Topology VLAN Latency Attenuation Packet Switching NAT IPv6 Asymmetric Encryption Firewall Digital Certificate

Common Misconceptions

  • Internet vs. Web: Confusing the physical infrastructure (Internet) with the service (WWW).
  • Switches vs. Routers: Believing they perform the same task; students must distinguish between MAC-based local delivery and IP-based global routing.
  • WiFi = Internet: Assuming a wireless connection inherently provides internet access, ignoring the role of the gateway.
  • Encryption: Thinking Symmetric encryption is "weak" rather than just having a different use-case (speed) compared to Asymmetric (key exchange).

Big Ideas to Consider

  • Standardisation as Shared Knowledge: Protocols are "agreements." How does the global reliance on a single set of rules (TCP/IP) reflect a consensus-based model of knowledge?
  • Digital Divide: Does the physical infrastructure of a network dictate who can "know" or participate in global society?
